title: Small Claims Court Cost: Filing Fees and Limits by State (2026)
description: Small claims filing fees and claim limits for all 50 states with official sources, plus service costs, recovering costs, collecting and lawyer rules.
h1: How much does small claims court cost?
summary: Small claims filing fees run from $20 (North Dakota, Montana) to $295 (Florida claims over $2,500), and many states charge more as the claim grows. Expect a separate service fee, often $15 to $90 per defendant. Claim limits range from $2,500 in Kentucky to $20,000 or more in states such as Texas, Utah and Minnesota; California, Michigan and Nebraska bar lawyers from representing parties at the hearing.
body:
What small claims court actually costs

For most people the bill has three parts: the court's filing fee, the cost of formally notifying (serving) the other side, and your own time. Filing fees range from a flat $20 in North Dakota and Montana to tiered schedules that reach $295 in Florida for claims above $2,500 [1][2][10]. Service usually adds a smaller second fee, for example $15 for California's clerk mail service, $12 for an officer in Virginia, $30 for the sheriff in North Carolina and $90 for a constable in Tarrant County, Texas [9][13][11][12].

Example (California, individual plaintiff): a $4,000 claim falls in the $1,500.01–$5,000 tier, so the filing fee is $50 [8]. Serving one defendant by clerk mail adds $15 [9]. Court cost: $50 + $15 = $65, before any time off work.

Claim limits vary just as much: $2,500 in Kentucky, $15,000 in North Dakota and $20,000 in Minnesota and Utah [3][1][4][5]; the table below covers every state. Some states also set a lower limit for businesses. California allows $12,500 for individuals but $6,250 for other plaintiffs, and Washington allows $10,000 for individuals and $5,000 for others [8][24]. In New York City, corporations cannot use small claims at all and must use the commercial claims part instead [23].

Small claims limits and filing fees in all 50 states

Fees below are what the plaintiff pays to file. Where a state uses tiers, the fee rises with the amount you claim. "Varies by county" means fees are set locally; call the clerk of the court where you will file. You can also estimate your fee with the small claims filing fee calculator.

Limits normally exclude interest and court costs, and a few states carve out exceptions, such as motor-vehicle property damage in Massachusetts or security-deposit claims in Connecticut and Hawaii. If your claim is above the limit, most courts make you either give up the excess or file in the regular civil division, where fees and procedures are heavier. Read the linked source for your state before filing.

Serving the other party

Filing does not notify the defendant. You must arrange service, and you pay for it up front. The common methods are certified mail sent by the clerk, a sheriff or constable, or a private process server.

  • Clerk mail: the cheapest option where it is offered. California charges $15 per defendant [9].
  • Sheriff or constable: $28 per Indiana service in the counties checked, $30 in North Carolina, and $90 per person served in Tarrant County, Texas [14][11][12].
  • Private process server: sets its own price; useful when the defendant avoids mail or the sheriff.

Budget for each defendant separately. Suing a business owner and the business is two defendants and usually two service fees.

Can you get your costs back if you win?

Usually you can ask the judge to add filing and service costs to the judgment. Nebraska's statute says service costs are added to the judgment, Hawaii's court brochure says the same, and Alaska lets you recover interest and court costs even above its $10,000 limit [15][16][25]. Your time off work, travel and copying are generally not recoverable. A judgment that includes costs is still only a piece of paper until the other side pays.

Collecting a judgment

Courts do not collect for you. If the defendant does not pay voluntarily, you use enforcement tools such as wage garnishment, a bank levy or a lien on property, and each step can carry its own fee. West Virginia magistrate courts charge $5 for each enforcement service such as an execution or garnishment, and Indiana counties charge another $28 for post-judgment sheriff service [17][14]. Before you sue, ask whether the defendant has a job, a bank account or property you could reach. A $3,000 judgment against someone with no income or assets can cost you more to chase than it returns.

Send a demand letter first

A short written demand often settles the matter without a filing fee. It also helps your case: California's claim form asks whether you demanded payment from the defendant where possible before filing [19]. A good demand letter states the amount owed, how you calculated it, a specific date to pay by and that you will file in small claims if it is not paid. Keep a copy and proof of delivery.

Checklist before you file

  • Is your claim under your state's limit, and are you allowed to file there (some states bar collection agencies or limit filings per year)?
  • Do you know the defendant's exact legal name and an address where they can be served?
  • Is the filing deadline (statute of limitations) still open?
  • Do you have documents: contract, invoices, photos, texts, repair estimates?
  • Can the defendant actually pay if you win?

Can you bring a lawyer to small claims?

It depends on the state, and several states say no:

  • California: "no attorney may take part in the conduct or defense of a small claims action," except attorneys suing or being sued for themselves or for all-attorney firms. Lawyers may still advise you before or after filing, and may represent you on appeal to superior court or in enforcing the judgment [18].
  • Michigan: an attorney may not take part in filing, prosecuting or defending a small claims case except on their own behalf [20].
  • Nebraska: no party may be represented by an attorney in small claims court, with limited exceptions [21].
  • Arkansas: if a defendant hires a lawyer, the case moves to the regular civil docket [22].

In many other states lawyers are allowed but rarely worth it on a small claim. Hourly billing is the issue: at Clio's national average of $349 an hour [26], even a short engagement eats into a modest recovery.

Example: 3 hours of preparation and 2 hours in court = 5 hours × $349 = $1,745 in fees to pursue a $3,000 claim. Unless a contract or statute lets you recover attorney fees from the other side, most of the win would go to the lawyer.

Paying for a one-time consultation to check your claim, or to prepare you for a defense, can still make sense. See what a lawyer consultation costs and, for larger disputes, how much a regular lawsuit costs.

If you cannot afford the fee

Most courts have a fee-waiver application for people with low income. Colorado publishes fee-waiver forms for small claims, and Kansas lets the judge waive the docket fee for good cause [6][7]. Ask the clerk for the form before you pay. Free help is also available through court self-help centers and legal aid; see our legal aid guide.

faq.q: How much does it cost to file in small claims court?
faq.a: It depends on your state and, in many states, on the amount you claim. Verified fees range from $20 in North Dakota and Montana to $295 for Florida claims over $2,500, plus a separate service fee, often $15 to $90 per defendant.

faq.q: Do I get my filing fee back if I win?
faq.a: Usually the judge can add your filing and service costs to the judgment, so the defendant owes them along with your claim. You still have to collect, and time off work is not reimbursed.

faq.q: What is the most I can sue for in small claims?
faq.a: Limits run from $2,500 in Kentucky to $25,000 in Tennessee General Sessions Court and Delaware Justice of the Peace Court. Several states set lower limits for businesses, such as $6,250 in California.

faq.q: Can a business sue in small claims court?
faq.a: In most states yes, sometimes with a lower dollar limit or a cap on how many claims it can file. New York City requires corporations to use the separate commercial claims part.

faq.q: Should I hire a lawyer for small claims?
faq.a: Some states, including California, Michigan and Nebraska, do not let lawyers represent parties at the hearing. Where it is allowed, hourly fees often exceed what a small claim is worth, so a single consultation is usually the better buy.
